content: Fletcher's Laxative, also known as Fletcher's Castoria, is an oral syrup that contains a stimulant laxative along with ingredients designed to soothe the stomach. The active ingredient concentration is 3 mg/mL. Other components of the formulation include citric acid, flavoring agents, glycerin, methylparaben, propylparaben, purified water, sodium benzoate, and sucrose. The product is non-alcoholic and available without a prescription. It typically produces a laxative effect within 6 to 12 hours of administration. There are no documented drug interactions; however, as a stimulant laxative, it may influence the duration that other medications remain in the digestive tract. It is recommended to avoid taking senna within 1 to 2 hours of consuming other medications. Caution is advised, as senna has the potential to be habit-forming with prolonged use. Fletcher's Castoria appears to have been rebranded as Fletcher's Laxative for Kids, with the original Castoria name no longer featured on the product's website. Although marketed as a children's laxative in the United States, it is also effective for adults. Once a common product in drugstores, it has become increasingly difficult to locate. The product has a long history, dating back to May 12, 1868, when Dr. Samuel Pitcher of Barnstable, Massachusetts, was granted a patent by the United States Patent Office for a cathartic formulation. This original remedy contained senna, sodium bicarbonate, essence of wintergreen, taraxacum, sugar, and water, and was initially sold under the name Pitcher's Castoria. Over time, the formula underwent modifications. In 1871, Charles Henry Fletcher, with financial backing from Demas Barnes, established The Centaur Company to acquire the rights to and manufacture Pitcher's Castoria. The product was subsequently renamed Fletcher's Castoria. It became the focus of one of the most significant early mass advertising campaigns. Advertisements for Castoria from the 1870s through the 1920s were prominently displayed on buildings in New York City and were still visible as late as the 1970s to 2005. At the opening of the Brooklyn Bridge in 1883, Castoria advertisements were ubiquitous, covering nearly every blank wall in sight. These ads are clearly visible in historical photographs of the bridge's inauguration. During World War II, two B-17 Flying Fortress bombers were named Fletcher's Castoria. Both were part of the 100th Bomb Group. The first aircraft was lost in action, though its crew survived, while the second survived the war. The latter was piloted by William H. Fletcher, who was not a descendant of Charles Henry Fletcher, but the aircraft was named in his honor. The Centaur Company was acquired by Sterling Drug, Inc., during the 1920s. Later, in 1988, the Japanese company Rohto purchased Mentholatum, a related brand.
